newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian privatisation seen favouring home control.
newsitem.headline: Russian privatisation seen favouring home control.

text.p: Russia is motoring ahead with a major privatisation programme, but economists believe foreign partners will be limited to portfolio investment stakes rather than offered the driver's seat at prime companies.

Russia says it will auction stakes in major companies such as Svyazinvest telecoms holding company and oil company LUKoil, and the government has discussed selling half of dominant automaker AvtoVAZ to help pay the company's back taxes.

The appointment of privatisation golden boy Anatoly Chubais as First Deputy Prime Minister has encouraged investors that Russia will move to a second wave of reform, which stalled last year during elections and President Boris Yeltsin's illness.
But economists say Russia is still struggling with its approach to privatisation.
"It is clear they are groping for (privatisation) strategy," said a Western diplomat. "Whether to attract technology or raise funds for the budget or attract local funds for restructuring."
Chubais spearheaded the shares-for-loans privatisation plan, criticised for insider deals, which traded control of government stakes in major companies for loans from commercial banks.
"If you go along one track to do reforms to attract investment but on the other go along with sweetheart deals, you are going to have a problem," the diplomat said.

Stephen O'Sullivan, head of research at MC Securities, said a Western-friendly reform team under Chubais could clean up the investment process but Russia would jealously guard control of its crown jewel companies.

"Even among Chubais's group there seems to be a mind-set that selling off assets cheaply to foreigners is not desirable," he said, adding Russian officials and management generally hoped to use Western money but maintain strategic control. "I wonder if Russia was ever interest in foreign strategic investors."
But O'Sullivan said Russia was rapidly developing an equity culture and companies privatising or restructuring would offer portfolio equity stakes rather than debt.
LUKoil, Russia's biggest oil producer, said last month the government would auction a 15 percent stake in the company targeted at portfolio investors later this year.
Russian and foreign investors will be offered chances for parts of a 49 percent stake in Svyazinvest after a deal with a potential strategic partner, Italy's Stet Spa, fell through.
Communications Minister Vladimir Bulgak has said a big foreign stake in Svyazinvest would threaten national security.
Kristen Burton Steiner, a telecoms analyst at Alfa-Capital investment bank, said that regional telecoms seeking funds to expand networks were generally wary of investors.
"Outerlying regionals are basically looking for financing for capital investment -- equipment providers," she said. But the companies are not interested in strategic investment.
"Many don't own their own shares and don't care about supporting the share price," she said.
But Chubais is respected for administrative skills and economists said his team could spark sell-offs -- or productivity gains -- in companies on the edge of bankruptcy.

The government last week ordered indebted companies to transfer controlling stakes in trust to the government or face bankruptcy. The companies must pay taxes on time or the government could sell the stakes.
United City Bank auto analyst Patricia Isayeva said Chubais would use such rules to force action at companies like car maker AvtoVAZ, which owes $500 million to the state.
Companies which fail to live up to their responsibilities could face a ruthless response -- and be sold, she said.

"The new governemnt is not interested in specific plans for specific companies," she said. "They are interested in the rules of the game. Managing is for management. But taxes and workers have to be paid, and it doesn't matter how you find the money."
